About

Over roughly seven and a half years in the pharmaceutical industry, including Quality Management Systems, I worked on CAPA, market complaints, SOP preparation and training activities. That work taught me why records must be accurate, processes traceable and conclusions supported by evidence.

I now apply the same discipline to business and data analysis: framing the question, preparing and validating data, and explaining what the evidence does and does not show. The move is a natural one, and it makes me especially useful for healthcare, pharmaceutical, quality, operations and compliance reporting.

What I bring

Quality and process perspective. Structured documentation, defined processes and data consistency.

Analytical capability. SQL, Excel and Power BI applied across six projects, supported by working knowledge of Python.

Business-oriented approach. Start from the question, then choose the analysis and state the limits.

SQL + Excel Dashboard

Beverage Sales

Which categories, cities and branches drive revenue? Joins, subqueries, CASE, TOP and a pivot-based dashboard.

  • SQL Server / SSMS
  • Excel PivotTables
9,971transactions
2SQL tables
17SQL queries

Business questions

  • Which product categories earn the most revenue?
  • How does average order value vary by city?
  • Which branches rank highest, and which beat the company average?
  • How do weekend and weekday revenue compare?

Dataset and fields

Two tables: branches (branch_id, branch_name, city) and sales (transaction_id, sale_date, branch_id, shop_name, product_id, product_category, unit_price, qty_sold, revenue, profit_margin, year, month, weekday). The Excel workbook holds 9,971 transaction records.

Analytical approach

Aggregation, joins, nested subqueries, NOT EXISTS, CASE tiers, TOP and combined WHERE, GROUP BY and ORDER BY.

SQL queries

Written in SQL Server (SSMS).

View all queries
-- ============================================================
-- BEVERAGE SALES ANALYSIS — SQL PORTFOLIO PROJECT
-- Author: Mehrosh Qureshi
-- Platform: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)
-- Tables used: branches (branch_id, branch_name, city)
--              sales    (transaction_id, sale_date, branch_id,
--                         shop_name, product_id, product_category,
--                         unit_price, qty_sold, revenue,
--                         profit_margin, year, month, weekday)
-- ============================================================


-- ============================================================
-- 1. BASIC EXPLORATION
-- ============================================================

-- 1.1 List all cities where branches are located
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM branches;

-- 1.2 Count total number of transactions
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_transactions FROM sales;

-- 1.3 Count how many times each product category was sold
SELECT product_category, COUNT(*) AS times_sold
FROM sales
GROUP BY product_category;


-- ============================================================
-- 2. AGGREGATION & REVENUE
-- ============================================================

-- 2.1 Total revenue generated by each product category
SELECT product_category, SUM(revenue) AS total_revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY product_category
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

-- 2.2 Average order value per city
SELECT branches.city, ROUND(AVG(sales.revenue),2) AS avg_order_value
FROM sales
JOIN branches ON sales.branch_id = branches.branch_id
GROUP BY branches.city;

-- 2.3 Total revenue across the entire business
SELECT SUM(revenue) AS total_revenue FROM sales;


-- ============================================================
-- 3. JOINS — BRANCH & CITY PERFORMANCE
-- ============================================================

-- 3.1 Revenue generated by every branch, city-wise
SELECT branches.city, branches.branch_name, SUM(sales.revenue) AS total_revenue
FROM sales
JOIN branches ON sales.branch_id = branches.branch_id
GROUP BY branches.city, branches.branch_name
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

-- 3.2 Cities whose total revenue crosses 500,000
SELECT city, total_revenue
FROM (
    SELECT branches.city, SUM(sales.revenue) AS total_revenue
    FROM sales JOIN branches ON sales.branch_id = branches.branch_id
    GROUP BY branches.city
) AS city_summary
WHERE total_revenue > 500000;


-- ============================================================
-- 4. SUBQUERIES
-- ============================================================

-- 4.1 Branches performing above the company-wide average revenue
SELECT branch_id, SUM(revenue) AS branch_revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY branch_id
HAVING SUM(revenue) > (SELECT AVG(revenue) FROM sales);

-- 4.2 City of the single highest-revenue branch (nested subquery)
SELECT city
FROM branches
WHERE branch_id = (
    SELECT TOP 1 branch_id FROM sales
    GROUP BY branch_id
    ORDER BY SUM(revenue) DESC
);

-- 4.3 Transactions priced above the overall average unit price
SELECT TOP 5 transaction_id, product_category, unit_price
FROM sales
WHERE unit_price > (SELECT AVG(unit_price) FROM sales)
ORDER BY unit_price DESC;

-- 4.4 Branches that have never sold a particular category (NOT EXISTS)
SELECT branches.branch_name
FROM branches
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM sales
    WHERE sales.branch_id = branches.branch_id AND sales.product_category = 'Iced Latte'
);


-- ============================================================
-- 5. CASE STATEMENTS
-- ============================================================

-- 5.1 Classify each product category into a profit margin tier
SELECT product_category,
    CASE
        WHEN AVG(profit_margin) >= 150 THEN 'High Margin'
        WHEN AVG(profit_margin) >= 80 THEN 'Medium Margin'
        ELSE 'Low Margin'
    END AS margin_tier
FROM sales
GROUP BY product_category;

-- 5.2 Compare total revenue on weekends vs weekdays
SELECT
    CASE WHEN weekday IN ('Sat','Sun') THEN 'Weekend' ELSE 'Weekday' END AS day_type,
    SUM(revenue) AS total_revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY CASE WHEN weekday IN ('Sat','Sun') THEN 'Weekend' ELSE 'Weekday' END;


-- ============================================================
-- 6. AGGREGATION WITH TOP
-- ============================================================

-- 6.1 Best-selling product category by quantity sold
SELECT TOP 1 product_category, SUM(qty_sold) AS total_qty
FROM sales
GROUP BY product_category
ORDER BY total_qty DESC;

-- 6.2 Top 3 branches by total revenue
SELECT TOP 3 branches.branch_name, SUM(sales.revenue) AS total_revenue
FROM sales JOIN branches ON sales.branch_id = branches.branch_id
GROUP BY branches.branch_name
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;


-- ============================================================
-- 7. WHERE + GROUP BY + ORDER BY COMBINED
-- ============================================================

-- 7.1 Revenue by city and category, restricted to bulk orders (qty >= 2)
SELECT branches.city, sales.product_category, SUM(sales.revenue) AS total_revenue, SUM(sales.qty_sold) AS total_qty
FROM sales
JOIN branches ON sales.branch_id = branches.branch_id
WHERE sales.qty_sold >= 2
GROUP BY branches.city, sales.product_category
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;

Dashboard and visuals

An interactive Excel dashboard built with PivotTables and PivotCharts accompanies the SQL work.

Key findings

Dashboard KPIs: 9,971 transactions, 14,117 units sold and 3,942,415 total revenue.

Insights and recommendations

  • Insight. Revenue is spread almost evenly across the five categories (19.0% to 21.0%). Masala Chai (21.0%) and Filter Coffee (20.6%) lead, and they also have the highest average profit margin value (about 135 against about 127 for the others).

    Recommendation. Give Masala Chai and Filter Coffee priority in promotion and stock, and review pricing on the lower-margin lines.

  • Insight. Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru together generate 69.9% of revenue, while Hyderabad is lowest at 12.0%.

    Recommendation. Check whether Hyderabad has fewer branches or weaker sales per branch before deciding where to invest.

  • Insight. Saturday and Sunday bring 33.1% of revenue from 2 of 7 days (28.6% if days were equal).

    Recommendation. Plan staffing and stock around weekend peaks, and test weekday offers to lift quieter days.

Business relevance

Turns transaction data into branch, city and category comparisons that a commercial team can use to decide where to focus.

Limitations and next steps

Exploratory practice, not a validated business conclusion.

SQL + Excel Dashboard

ADR Data

What reporting patterns appear in adverse drug reaction reports? CTEs, ranking and year-on-year window functions.

  • SQL Server / SSMS
  • Excel PivotTables
6,102report records
897drugs
70countries

Business questions

  • How many reports are filed each year, and how has that changed?
  • Which drugs, countries and age groups appear most often?
  • What share of reports is flagged serious?
  • How do early and recent periods compare?

Dataset and fields

Two tables: drugs (drug_id, drug_name) and adr_reports (report_id, year, serious_flag, reactions, reaction_outcome, patient_recovered, drug_id, drug_indication, age_group, patient_sex, country).

Analytical approach

Joins, subqueries, CASE severity tiers, CTEs, ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG and LEAD.

SQL queries

Written in SQL Server (SSMS).

View all queries
-- ============================================================
-- ADVERSE DRUG REACTION (ADR) ANALYSIS — SQL PORTFOLIO PROJECT
-- Author: Mehrosh Qureshi
-- Platform: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)
-- Tables used: drugs       (drug_id, drug_name)
--              adr_reports (report_id, year, serious_flag, reactions,
--                            reaction_outcome, patient_recovered,
--                            drug_id, drug_indication, age_group,
--                            patient_sex, country)
-- ============================================================


-- ============================================================
-- 1. BASIC EXPLORATION
-- ============================================================

-- 1.1 List all countries that reported an adverse reaction
SELECT DISTINCT country FROM adr_reports;

-- 1.2 Count total number of ADR reports
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_reports FROM adr_reports;

-- 1.3 Count reports by patient age group
SELECT age_group, COUNT(*) AS report_count
FROM adr_reports
GROUP BY age_group;


-- ============================================================
-- 2. AGGREGATION & REPORTING METRICS
-- ============================================================

-- 2.1 Number of reports filed each year
SELECT year, COUNT(*) AS report_count
FROM adr_reports
GROUP BY year
ORDER BY year;

-- 2.2 Patients recovered vs not recovered
SELECT patient_recovered, COUNT(*) AS report_count
FROM adr_reports
GROUP BY patient_recovered;

-- 2.3 Total reports flagged as serious (any flag other than None)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS serious_reports
FROM adr_reports
WHERE serious_flag <> 'None';


-- ============================================================
-- 3. JOINS — DRUG-LEVEL REPORTING
-- ============================================================

-- 3.1 Number of reports filed against each drug
SELECT drugs.drug_name, COUNT(*) AS report_count
FROM adr_reports
JOIN drugs ON adr_reports.drug_id = drugs.drug_id
GROUP BY drugs.drug_name
ORDER BY report_count DESC;

-- 3.2 Drugs with more than 50 reports filed against them
SELECT drug_name, report_count
FROM (
    SELECT drugs.drug_name, COUNT(*) AS report_count
    FROM adr_reports JOIN drugs ON adr_reports.drug_id = drugs.drug_id
    GROUP BY drugs.drug_name
) AS drug_summary
WHERE report_count > 50;


-- ============================================================
-- 4. SUBQUERIES
-- ============================================================

-- 4.1 Drugs with report counts above the average per drug
SELECT drug_id, COUNT(*) AS drug_report_count
FROM adr_reports
GROUP BY drug_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > (
    SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM adr_reports GROUP BY drug_id) AS t
);

-- 4.2 Country that filed the single highest number of reports
SELECT TOP 1 country, COUNT(*) AS report_count
FROM adr_reports
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY report_count DESC;

-- 4.3 Countries reporting above the average report count per country
SELECT country, report_count
FROM (
    SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS report_count FROM adr_reports GROUP BY country
) AS t
WHERE report_count > (
    SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM adr_reports GROUP BY country) AS t2
);

-- 4.4 Drugs that have never been linked to a death (NOT EXISTS)
SELECT DISTINCT drugs.drug_name
FROM drugs
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM adr_reports
    WHERE adr_reports.drug_id = drugs.drug_id AND adr_reports.serious_flag LIKE '%Death%'
);


-- ============================================================
-- 5. CASE STATEMENTS
-- ============================================================

-- 5.1 Classify each report into a severity tier
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN serious_flag LIKE '%Death%' THEN 'Critical'
        WHEN serious_flag = 'None' THEN 'Non-Serious'
        ELSE 'Serious'
    END AS severity_tier,
    COUNT(*) AS report_count
FROM adr_reports
GROUP BY
    CASE
        WHEN serious_flag LIKE '%Death%' THEN 'Critical'
        WHEN serious_flag = 'None' THEN 'Non-Serious'
        ELSE 'Serious'
    END;

-- 5.2 Compare reports filed in the early period vs the recent period
SELECT
    CASE WHEN year <= 2016 THEN 'Early Period' ELSE 'Recent Period' END AS period,
    COUNT(*) AS report_count
FROM adr_reports
GROUP BY CASE WHEN year <= 2016 THEN 'Early Period' ELSE 'Recent Period' END;


-- ============================================================
-- 6. AGGREGATION WITH TOP
-- ============================================================

-- 6.1 Drug with the highest number of reports filed against it
SELECT TOP 1 drugs.drug_name, COUNT(*) AS report_count
FROM adr_reports JOIN drugs ON adr_reports.drug_id = drugs.drug_id
GROUP BY drugs.drug_name
ORDER BY report_count DESC;

-- 6.2 Top 3 countries by number of reports filed
SELECT TOP 3 country, COUNT(*) AS report_count
FROM adr_reports
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY report_count DESC;


-- ============================================================
-- 7. WHERE + GROUP BY + ORDER BY COMBINED
-- ============================================================

-- 7.1 Serious reports by country and drug indication
SELECT country, drug_indication, COUNT(*) AS report_count
FROM adr_reports
WHERE serious_flag <> 'None'
GROUP BY country, drug_indication
ORDER BY report_count DESC;


-- ============================================================
-- 8. WINDOW FUNCTIONS & CTE
-- ============================================================

-- 8.1 Top 5 drugs by report count, numbered with ROW_NUMBER
WITH drug_ranking AS (
    SELECT drugs.drug_name, COUNT(*) AS report_count,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS row_num
    FROM adr_reports
    JOIN drugs ON adr_reports.drug_id = drugs.drug_id
    GROUP BY drugs.drug_name
)
SELECT drug_name, report_count, row_num FROM drug_ranking WHERE row_num <= 5;

-- 8.2 Top 3 countries by report count, ranked with RANK (ties share a rank)
WITH country_ranking AS (
    SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS report_count,
           RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rank_num
    FROM adr_reports
    GROUP BY country
)
SELECT country, report_count, rank_num FROM country_ranking WHERE rank_num <= 3;

-- 8.3 Age groups ranked by report count with DENSE_RANK (no gaps after ties)
WITH age_ranking AS (
    SELECT age_group, COUNT(*) AS report_count,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS dense_rank_num
    FROM adr_reports
    GROUP BY age_group
)
SELECT age_group, report_count, dense_rank_num FROM age_ranking ORDER BY dense_rank_num;

-- 8.4 Reports filed this year vs. the previous year (LAG)
SELECT year, report_count,
       LAG(report_count) OVER (ORDER BY year) AS prev_year_reports
FROM (
    SELECT year, COUNT(*) AS report_count FROM adr_reports GROUP BY year
) AS t;

-- 8.5 Reports filed this year vs. the following year (LEAD)
SELECT year, report_count,
       LEAD(report_count) OVER (ORDER BY year) AS next_year_reports
FROM (
    SELECT year, COUNT(*) AS report_count FROM adr_reports GROUP BY year
) AS t;

Dashboard and visuals

An interactive Excel dashboard built with PivotTables and PivotCharts accompanies the SQL work.

Key findings

Dashboard KPIs: 6,102 reports; the most reported drug is Avandia (2,178 reactions). These are report counts only.

Insights and recommendations

  • Insight. All 6,102 reports carry a serious flag. Hospitalisation appears in 37.5% of reports and death in 10.2% (620 reports).

    Recommendation. Treat this as a serious-case dataset: do not estimate overall seriousness rates from it, and use the outcome categories to prioritise review.

  • Insight. Reports are concentrated: the US supplies 4,337 (71.1%), and Avandia (931 reports, 15.3%) and Adalimumab (712, 11.7%) are the top two drugs.

    Recommendation. Check whether this reflects real use, reporting systems or the data source before comparing countries or drugs.

  • Insight. Annual counts are very uneven (3,391 in 2016 against 608 in 2017), which looks more like differences in data coverage than a real trend.

    Recommendation. Verify data completeness for each year before reading any trend.

Business relevance

Pharmacovigilance-style reporting data sits close to my pharmaceutical background; structured counting by drug, country and severity is the first step towards signal review.

Limitations and next steps

Report counts alone do not establish causality, incidence or comparative safety risk. Findings are exploratory, not clinical conclusions.

SQL + Excel Dashboard

Diabetes Risk Analysis

How do glucose, BMI and risk scores vary across patient groups? Banding, ranking and age-group trend comparisons.

  • SQL Server / SSMS
  • Excel PivotTables
100,000patient records
14source fields

Business questions

  • How do average BMI and HbA1c differ by risk category and diabetes status?
  • Which age groups have a diabetes rate above the overall average?
  • Who are the highest-risk patients in each category?
  • How does average glucose change across age groups?

Dataset and fields

One patients table (patient_id, gender, age, hypertension, heart_disease, smoking_history, bmi, hba1c_level, blood_glucose_level, diabetes, plus derived age, health, glucose and risk categories).

Analytical approach

CASE banding, subqueries, CTEs, ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, LAG and LEAD.

SQL queries

Written in SQL Server (SSMS).

View all queries
-- ============================================================
-- DIABETES RISK ANALYSIS — SQL PORTFOLIO PROJECT
-- Author: Mehrosh Qureshi
-- Platform: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)
-- Table used: patients (patient_id, gender, age, hypertension,
--             heart_disease, smoking_history, bmi, hba1c_level,
--             blood_glucose_level, diabetes, age_group,
--             health_category, glucose_category, risk_score,
--             risk_category)
-- ============================================================


-- ============================================================
-- 1. BASIC EXPLORATION
-- ============================================================

-- 1.1 List all age groups in the dataset
SELECT DISTINCT age_group FROM patients;

-- 1.2 Count total number of patients
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_patients FROM patients;

-- 1.3 Count patients by gender
SELECT gender, COUNT(*) AS patient_count
FROM patients
GROUP BY gender;


-- ============================================================
-- 2. AGGREGATION
-- ============================================================

-- 2.1 Average BMI by risk category
SELECT risk_category, ROUND(AVG(bmi),2) AS avg_bmi
FROM patients
GROUP BY risk_category;

-- 2.2 Average HbA1c level by diabetes status
SELECT diabetes, ROUND(AVG(hba1c_level),2) AS avg_hba1c
FROM patients
GROUP BY diabetes;

-- 2.3 Count of patients with hypertension
SELECT COUNT(*) AS hypertension_count
FROM patients
WHERE hypertension = 1;


-- ============================================================
-- 3. CASE STATEMENTS
-- ============================================================

-- 3.1 Classify patients into a glucose band
SELECT
    CASE
        WHEN blood_glucose_level < 100 THEN 'Low'
        WHEN blood_glucose_level <= 140 THEN 'Normal'
        ELSE 'High'
    END AS glucose_band,
    COUNT(*) AS patient_count
FROM patients
GROUP BY
    CASE
        WHEN blood_glucose_level < 100 THEN 'Low'
        WHEN blood_glucose_level <= 140 THEN 'Normal'
        ELSE 'High'
    END;

-- 3.2 Classify patients into a broad age band
SELECT
    CASE WHEN age < 40 THEN 'Younger Adult' ELSE 'Older Adult' END AS age_band,
    COUNT(*) AS patient_count
FROM patients
GROUP BY CASE WHEN age < 40 THEN 'Younger Adult' ELSE 'Older Adult' END;


-- ============================================================
-- 4. SUBQUERIES
-- ============================================================

-- 4.1 Number of patients with BMI above the overall average
SELECT COUNT(*) AS above_avg_bmi_count
FROM patients
WHERE bmi > (SELECT AVG(bmi) FROM patients);

-- 4.2 Age groups with a diabetes rate above the overall average
SELECT age_group, diabetes_rate
FROM (
    SELECT age_group, AVG(diabetes) * 100 AS diabetes_rate FROM patients GROUP BY age_group
) AS t
WHERE diabetes_rate > (SELECT AVG(diabetes) * 100 FROM patients);

-- 4.3 Risk categories whose average glucose exceeds the overall average
SELECT risk_category, AVG(blood_glucose_level) AS avg_glucose
FROM patients
GROUP BY risk_category
HAVING AVG(blood_glucose_level) > (SELECT AVG(blood_glucose_level) FROM patients);


-- ============================================================
-- 5. WINDOW FUNCTIONS — ROW_NUMBER
-- ============================================================

-- 5.1 Top 3 patients per risk category, ranked by HbA1c level
SELECT patient_id, risk_category, hba1c_level, rn
FROM (
    SELECT patient_id, risk_category, hba1c_level,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY risk_category ORDER BY hba1c_level DESC) AS rn
    FROM patients
) AS ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;

-- 5.2 Overall top 10 patients by risk score
SELECT patient_id, risk_score, rn
FROM (
    SELECT patient_id, risk_score,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY risk_score DESC) AS rn
    FROM patients
) AS ranked
WHERE rn <= 10;


-- ============================================================
-- 6. WINDOW FUNCTIONS — RANK & DENSE_RANK
-- ============================================================

-- 6.1 Rank age groups by average glucose level (RANK)
SELECT age_group, avg_glucose, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY avg_glucose DESC) AS glucose_rank
FROM (
    SELECT age_group, AVG(blood_glucose_level) AS avg_glucose FROM patients GROUP BY age_group
) AS t;

-- 6.2 Rank risk categories by average BMI (DENSE_RANK)
SELECT risk_category, avg_bmi, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY avg_bmi DESC) AS bmi_rank
FROM (
    SELECT risk_category, AVG(bmi) AS avg_bmi FROM patients GROUP BY risk_category
) AS t;


-- ============================================================
-- 7. WINDOW FUNCTIONS — LEAD & LAG
-- ============================================================

-- 7.1 Compare each age group's average glucose to the previous age group (LAG)
SELECT age_group, avg_glucose,
       LAG(avg_glucose) OVER (ORDER BY
           CASE age_group WHEN '<30' THEN 1 WHEN '30-39' THEN 2 WHEN '40-49' THEN 3
                WHEN '50-59' THEN 4 WHEN '60+' THEN 5 END) AS prev_age_group_glucose
FROM (
    SELECT age_group, AVG(blood_glucose_level) AS avg_glucose FROM patients GROUP BY age_group
) AS t;

-- 7.2 Compare each age group's average HbA1c to the next age group (LEAD)
SELECT age_group, avg_hba1c,
       LEAD(avg_hba1c) OVER (ORDER BY
           CASE age_group WHEN '<30' THEN 1 WHEN '30-39' THEN 2 WHEN '40-49' THEN 3
                WHEN '50-59' THEN 4 WHEN '60+' THEN 5 END) AS next_age_group_hba1c
FROM (
    SELECT age_group, AVG(hba1c_level) AS avg_hba1c FROM patients GROUP BY age_group
) AS t;

-- 7.3 Show previous and next age group's average risk score (LAG + LEAD together)
SELECT age_group, avg_risk_score,
       LAG(avg_risk_score) OVER (ORDER BY age_rank) AS prev_risk_score,
       LEAD(avg_risk_score) OVER (ORDER BY age_rank) AS next_risk_score
FROM (
    SELECT age_group, AVG(risk_score) AS avg_risk_score,
           CASE age_group WHEN '<30' THEN 1 WHEN '30-39' THEN 2 WHEN '40-49' THEN 3
                WHEN '50-59' THEN 4 WHEN '60+' THEN 5 END AS age_rank
    FROM patients GROUP BY age_group
) AS t;


-- ============================================================
-- 8. CTE + WINDOW FUNCTIONS COMBINED
-- ============================================================

-- 8.1 Rank risk categories by total diabetes count, using a CTE + RANK
WITH risk_summary AS (
    SELECT risk_category, SUM(diabetes) AS diabetes_count
    FROM patients
    GROUP BY risk_category
)
SELECT risk_category, diabetes_count, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY diabetes_count DESC) AS rnk
FROM risk_summary;

-- 8.2 Age groups where average glucose is rising vs. the previous group (CTE + LAG)
WITH age_glucose AS (
    SELECT age_group, AVG(blood_glucose_level) AS avg_glucose
    FROM patients GROUP BY age_group
),
trend AS (
    SELECT age_group, avg_glucose,
           avg_glucose - LAG(avg_glucose) OVER (ORDER BY
               CASE age_group WHEN '<30' THEN 1 WHEN '30-39' THEN 2 WHEN '40-49' THEN 3
                    WHEN '50-59' THEN 4 WHEN '60+' THEN 5 END) AS change_from_prev
    FROM age_glucose
)
SELECT age_group, avg_glucose, change_from_prev FROM trend WHERE change_from_prev > 0;

Dashboard and visuals

An interactive Excel dashboard built with PivotTables and PivotCharts accompanies the SQL work.

Key findings

The dashboard summary reads: medium risk is the dominant category, and age, gender and glucose category collectively influence patient risk patterns.

Insights and recommendations

  • Insight. Diabetes prevalence in the dataset is 8.5% and rises steeply with age: 0.8% under 30, 3.3% at 30-39, 6.8% at 40-49, 12.5% at 50-59 and 19.7% at 60 and above.

    Recommendation. In this population, focus screening and awareness on people aged 50 and above.

  • Insight. HbA1c of 6.5 or more goes with a 36.8% diabetes rate, against 1.5% below 5.7. A BMI of 30 or more shows 18.0%, against 3.9% for a BMI of 18.5-25.

    Recommendation. Combine HbA1c, BMI and age into a single risk flag instead of looking at each measure alone.

  • Insight. Hypertension (27.9% against 6.9%) and heart disease (32.1% against 7.5%) are both linked to much higher diabetes rates.

    Recommendation. Include these comorbidities in risk scoring. This is an educational analysis and not clinical guidance.

Business relevance

Practises grouping and ranking health measures so patterns across patient groups can be explained clearly to non-technical readers.

Limitations and next steps

Educational analysis only. It does not diagnose, predict disease or support clinical decisions.

Finance Analysis

How do transactions, channels and risk indicators behave? Data model, measures and interactive visuals.

  • Power BI
  • DAX
  • Power Query
50,000transactions
5,000customers
15fields

Business questions

  • How does transaction value change over time?
  • Which channels and merchant categories dominate?
  • How do fees, taxes and risk scores relate to transaction status?
  • How does Total Amount compare with the prior year?

Dataset and fields

Transactions dataset: transaction_id, date, account, customer, type, channel, merchant_category, amount, fee, tax, currency, status, fraud flag, risk score, reference number. A customers table (5,000 customers) adds gender, city, state, occupation, segment and income.

Analytical approach

A data model linking finance_transactions, customers and a Calendar table, with measures for Total Amount, PY Amount, YoY Amount and YoY %. The report page holds KPI cards, a combo chart of Total vs PY Amount by month, a bar chart by merchant category, a donut by transaction status and a customer-segment table (amount, fee, tax, risk score), with slicers for gender, state, occupation, channel and year.

Dashboard and visuals

Key findings

Total Amount of 45.55 Cr (INR) across 50,000 transactions, with Rent the largest merchant category by amount.

Insights and recommendations

  • Insight. Failed transactions account for 10.4% of total value and pending ones for 4.2%.

    Recommendation. Investigate failure reasons. Failure rates are highest on ATM (10.9%) and Auto Debit (10.8%) and lowest on Net Banking (9.6%), so start there.

  • Insight. Annual totals are flat: 2023 at 137.1M, 2024 at 135.6M (-1.1%) and 2025 at 137.5M (+1.4%).

    Recommendation. Look for growth levers beyond volume, such as fees and category mix, since overall spend is not growing.

  • Insight. Retail makes up 54.5% of amount and 54.1% of customers, so spend per customer is similar across segments.

    Recommendation. Segment on spend or behaviour instead, because the current segments do not separate high-value customers.

Business relevance

Shows how transaction, fee and risk data can be modelled and reported for finance and operations stakeholders.

Limitations and next steps

State whether the report is complete, and credit any tutorial that inspired it.

Air Quality

How do air-quality indicators vary across cities and dates? Pivot-based dashboard with interactive controls.

  • Excel
  • PivotTables
24,850daily records
10source fields

Business questions

  • What is the average AQI by city?
  • How do pollutant measurements compare?
  • Which observations are highest and lowest?

Dataset and fields

City-day air-quality records: City, Date, PM2.5, PM10, NO2, CO, AQI and AQI_Bucket, with Year and Month derived. The workbook holds 24,850 daily records across major Indian cities.

Analytical approach

PivotTables and PivotCharts with slicers, a KPI header, and city and year-wise AQI comparisons.

Dashboard and visuals

Key findings

Dashboard KPIs: average AQI 166.46; highest AQI city Ahmedabad; lowest AQI city Aizawl (13); major pollutant PM10 at 118.45.

Insights and recommendations

  • Insight. Ahmedabad has the highest average AQI (452) and Aizawl the lowest (35). Poor, Very Poor or Severe days make up 25.9% of all readings.

    Recommendation. Prioritise pollution-control action in the most affected cities, starting with Ahmedabad, Delhi and Patna.

  • Insight. Air quality is seasonal: November (242), January (232) and December (227) average about twice July (112).

    Recommendation. Build seasonal action plans and public advisories for October to February.

  • Insight. The yearly average AQI falls from 212 in 2015 to 114 in 2020.

    Recommendation. Check city coverage and data completeness for each year before crediting any policy or cause for the decline.

Business relevance

Shows how environmental trends can be communicated to non-technical readers.

Limitations and next steps

Validate the workbook before publishing any KPI.

Power BI

Ecom Sales Dashboard

My first Power BI project: an e-commerce sales dashboard covering sales, profit, quantity and order value across categories, states and customers.

  • Power BI
500orders
1,500line items

Business questions

  • What are the total amount, profit, quantity and average order value?
  • Which sub-categories earn the most profit?
  • How does profit vary by month?
  • Which states and customers contribute the most amount?
  • How is quantity split by category and payment mode?

Dataset and fields

Two related tables: Orders (customer name, state, order date) and Details (amount, profit, quantity, category, sub-category, payment mode).

Analytical approach

Orders and Details were related in a data model with a date hierarchy. The report page has four KPI cards (amount, profit, quantity, average order value), profit by sub-category, profit by month, quantity by category and by payment mode, amount by state and by customer, and slicers for state and quarter.

Dashboard and visuals

Key findings

Across 500 orders and 1,500 line items: Amount 437,771, Profit 36,963 and Quantity 5,615. Printers is the top sub-category by profit and Maharashtra the top state by amount.

Insights and recommendations

  • Insight. Electronics earns the most amount (166,267) but the lowest profit margin (7.9%), while Clothing has the highest (9.2%).

    Recommendation. Review electronics pricing and discounts, and grow Clothing where margin is stronger.

  • Insight. 35.3% of line items (529 of 1,500) make a loss, and 5 sub-categories are loss-making overall, including Furnishings (-806) and Electronic Games (-644).

    Recommendation. Review costs and discounts on loss-making lines and consider dropping or repricing them.

  • Insight. Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh bring 43.4% of amount, and cash on delivery makes up 43.7% of quantity.

    Recommendation. Expand in under-served states and encourage UPI or card payment to reduce reliance on cash on delivery.

Business relevance

Shows how order-level data can be turned into a single view of sales, profit and customer contribution for a commercial team.

Limitations and next steps

As my first project, it is a learning build. Next steps: calculate average order value as total amount divided by number of orders rather than summing it, and show monthly profit with a column or line chart instead of a 100% stacked column.

Business Analysis sample

Sample Requirements Document: CAPA Tracking Dashboard

A sample I wrote to show how I document requirements, using my Pharma QMS background. It is not a system I built at an employer.

  • In one minute. Quality teams need one clear view of open events, slow closures and repeat issues. This document sets out what that dashboard should show, who uses it and what is still missing before it can be built.

The problem

Quality events and CAPA records are often spread across systems and spreadsheets. Leaders cannot easily see what is open, what is late and what keeps recurring, and reports take manual effort. (These are assumed pain points.)

Who needs it

  • QA Head: sponsor and main user.
  • Site QA managers: weekly review.
  • CAPA owners: action and closure.

What it must do

#The dashboard mustPriority
R1Show open events by site, risk level and event typeMust
R2Show average closure days by risk levelMust
R3Show on-time closure %Must
R4Show root causes and repeat eventsShould
R5Let users filter by date, site and event type, and open the event listMust
R6Highlight overdue itemsShould

User stories

  • As a QA head, I want to see all open high-risk events by site, so that I can prioritise my weekly review. Done when: every open High or Critical event is listed, with its age in days.

  • As a CAPA owner, I want to see my overdue items, so that I can close them on time. Done when: items past their target date appear in a separate list for the owner.

Process: before and after

Before (assumed)

  1. Event logged in the QMS
  2. Data copied to spreadsheets
  3. Monthly review

After

  1. Event logged in the QMS
  2. Data refreshes automatically
  3. Weekly review from the dashboard

Gap and risk

  • Gap: the quality event data I used to prepare this sample has no target closure date, so on-time closure (R3) and overdue items (R6) cannot be measured until that field is added.
  • Risk: status and root-cause values may differ between sites. A controlled list and a one-time data clean-up would address this.
